title: Top-$k$ Retrieval Leaves Memory Value Undetermined
trick: Treat the retrieval log as an undesigned experiment: with a fixed retrieval size, raising every memory's value and lowering the baseline fits every outcome equally, so no memory value is identifiable however long the log.
framing_stripped: Called 'LEDGER' and 'treating the history as an experiment that nobody designed'; it is (a) the classical estimability test for a linear functional under a rank-deficient design (Rao 1973: the coefficient vector must lie in the row space of the design matrix) applied to the 0/1 episode-by-memory retrieval matrix, with the observation that the Gram matrix of that design is just the retrieval and co-retrieval counts (eq. 1); (b) three corollaries naming the kernel vector that each common retrieval convention puts in the design: fixed size $k$ (Theorem 1), one private store per question (Proposition 2), memories always retrieved together (aliasing); (c) an audit of fourteen memory benchmarks' logs that needs no reader call and finds zero determined values in all 55 configurations (Table 2); and (d) a ridge fit with per-functional Gaussian intervals (eq. 5) plus a count-based retrieval heuristic that varies $k$ and fills about 40% of each set with the least-retrieved of the 20 most similar memories (eq. 8), which lifts the fraction determined on pooled HotpotQA from 0.001 to 0.797 at $-2.6$ accuracy points and gives $+2.7$ on LoCoMo.

load_bearing_assumption: Assumption 2 at $d=1$ for every positive number: the query-averaged value has no joint dividends above order one, so a memory's 'value' is its additive main effect $\theta_{\{i\}}$ and no pair of memories helps only together. The negative result survives violation (a memory undetermined at $d$ is undetermined at every higher $d$, Lemma B.3), but the 0.797 determined, every interval and every merge are $d=1$ numbers on multi-hop QA (HotpotQA questions have two gold passages), which is exactly where order-2 dividends live; the paper concedes 'Omitted dividends bias the estimates wherever they correlate with the design', and at $d=2$ the design has $p_2\approx4.4\times10^{6}$ columns against $T=7{,}200$, so $d=2$ is studied on synthetic logs only. Second, exogeneity: retrieval reads the query, so the per-query deviation $\delta_{q_t}(S_t)$ can correlate with the design, and 'The reported values are associational unless the log is exogenous (Appendix H.1)'. Third, Proposition 3 needs 'the retrieved sets do not depend on past outcomes', which every bandit-style or RL memory policy violates; the valid alternative (Abbasi-Yadkori et al. 2011) is 6.6 to 36 times as wide in the paper's own synthetic study.
weakest_component: The remedy, not the theorem. (1) The retrieval rule is admitted to be a heuristic: 'LEDGER's rule is a count-based heuristic motivated by $A$-optimal design; it optimises no criterion', 'The rule treats the $M=20$ memories most similar to the query as candidates of comparable relevance, and we did not test this assumption directly', and the pre-registration called it $A$-optimal tie-breaking while the run used eq. 8 (Appendix G.4). (2) Its cost: the pre-registered claim 'Instrumentation is approximately free' was withdrawn ($-2.6$ points on 1,600 pooled HotpotQA questions, $[-4.2,-0.9]$, $p=0.004$); 'the only rule that removes the cost is an oracle that needs gold labels', and the pre-registered label-free gate (top-1 similarity below median) failed its rule ($+1.25$ $[0.0,+2.4]$ against ungated LEDGER). (3) The remedy transfers poorly: the pre-registered test 'The remedy recovers identifiability on three audited benchmarks' failed (fractions 0.46, 0.13, 0.08 against floors 0.50, 0.22, 0.13; 'falsified on MemoryAgentBench'), 'Reach is the binding ceiling' 'failed on two of three benchmarks', and on LoCoMo score perturbation at $\beta=0.10$ determines 0.532 against LEDGER's 0.321 (Appendix F.2). (4) The determined values have not yet bought a better store: on synthetic logs with 40 memories, ranking undetermined memories last and keeping 30% of the store, the retained store succeeds in 5.52 of 300 evaluation episodes under LEDGER against 7.14 under reward averaging and 6.48 under the true Shapley values (Appendix F.7), and 'the pre-registered real-data retention test was not completed'. (5) Coverage: measured on synthetic logs only ('on real logs it cannot be measured'), and the headline $d=2$ coverage on reported values is a post hoc restriction after the pre-registered test fell to 0.572 (Appendix G.3); the sample-complexity bound was withdrawn (slope 0.82 against a rule of 1.00). (6) Evidence base: one author, hosted readers that 'cannot be pinned', exact match with the same model as judge, pooled stores that are the author's own construction (pooling costs 15.7 points on LongMemEval against each question's own store). (7) The ten-minute dismissal: the identifiability condition is Rao's estimability and the aliasing is textbook factorial design; the contribution is the mapping (Gram matrix = retrieval counts) and the audit, which the paper itself says ('The condition that decides identifiability is classical').
regime: Theory: any $n$, $T$, $d$; real-data identifiability at $d=1$ only; $d=2$ on synthetic logs (36 settings of $n$, $k$, $T$, $\lambda$, 20 random designs each). Audit: 14 memory benchmarks, 55 configurations, $k\in\{3,5,10\}$ plus 'all' for four long-context benchmarks, one pass each, no reader call; e.g. HotpotQA $T=300$, $n=2{,}971$, 300 blocks; MultiHopRAG $T=2{,}556$, $n=23{,}078$, shared store, 269 to 15 blocks; HELMET $T=356$, $n=40{,}000$, 41 blocks; 0 determined everywhere (Table 2). Retrieval experiments: pooled HotpotQA, fraction determined on 300 questions over 24 passes ($n=2{,}971$, $T=7{,}200$, sizes $\{3,5,8\}$, five seeds), accuracy on 1,600 held-out questions against a 15,900-memory pooled store; LoCoMo 1,542 questions (top-$k$ 0.191 vs LEDGER 0.217) and two conversations with $n=788$, $T=1{,}440$ for fractions; LongMemEval 479 questions (0.263 vs 0.271). Memories are turn- or paragraph-level spans; encoder all-MiniLM-L6-v2, cosine similarity; reader gemini-2.5-flash-lite at temperature 0, up to 24,000 characters of context; exact match, else same-model judge; gemini-3.6-flash and gemini-3.7-flash only for the pooling-cost measurement. Statistics: paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples) and paired permutation (10,000 sign flips), Holm over the four random-rule comparisons; every claim pre-registered, three withdrawn, one post hoc. Compute: hosted API calls only; dollars and tokens not reported (unknown, not in text). Single author (Illinois Institute of Technology), arXiv cs.AI, posted 2026-11-02, anonymous code link (under review); no training of any model.
information_asymmetry: (1) Retrieval-decision time vs log-reading time. The retrieval log holds, for every episode, the set and the outcome, but under relevance ranking at a fixed size it cannot contain the variation that separates one memory's contribution from the baseline (the kernel vector $\mathbf{h}_\emptyset$: 'adding the same amount to every value and removing twice that amount from the baseline leaves every predicted outcome unchanged: the history fixes only the differences between values') or from an always-co-retrieved partner ($\mathbf{e}_{\{i\}}-\mathbf{e}_{\{j\}}$). That variation exists only at the moment of retrieval, where the agent could choose a different set size or a less-retrieved partner; 'Every invisible change can be found from the log before any value is estimated, and a change to retrieval can remove it.' What the retrieval log cannot determine: at $d=1$, any single $\varphi_i$ under fixed $k$ (only differences $\theta_{\{i\}}-\theta_{\{j\}}$ are determined), more than $T_b$ values per private store of $n_b$ memories asked $T_b$ times, and the split of a tied group's total. What a designed log determines: with a shared store, at least $d+1$ distinct sizes and non-nested sets, every dividend of order at most $d$; the paper's statement of why designed ablations work is 'independent random subsets vary in size and are not nested, so with enough of them $\mathbf{X}_{1}$ has full column rank, while the logs that retrieval produces under a fixed size have a nonzero kernel at every $T$'. The measured price of design is $-2.6$ accuracy points on pooled HotpotQA for LEDGER's rule, 13.3 to 37.0 points for fully random rules reaching 0.98 or more determined, and $+2.7$ on LoCoMo where top-$k$ finds only 0.24 of the gold memories. (2) Outcome-free vs outcome-dependent. Whether a value is determined is decided by the counts alone: 'The retrieval convention that produces these counts therefore decides which memory values a log can determine, before any outcome is observed and whatever the memories contain.' (sec. 3); the audit calls no reader. So the question 'can this log value its memories at all' is answerable on any deployed system's retrieval trace for free, before anyone pays for outcomes or judges. (3) Need vs contribution. Access frequency, which proxy memory managers (FadeMem, budget-curated forgetting) score on, is the diagonal of $\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}$: 'a memory retrieved in every episode of a top-$k$ log has the largest frequency and an undetermined value'. (4) Training-time design vs learned credit. For RL memory agents the rollouts are the log and the reward the outcome; 'When rollouts retrieve a fixed number of memories, the rewards leave every memory's credit undetermined (Theorem 1), so a learned per-memory value is fixed by the learner and not by the rewards'; the rollout policy, set at training time, decides what the reward can teach. (5) Scope the paper claims: 'The same test therefore applies to the tools an agent calls in an episode, the passages a retrieval-augmented generator reads, and the slates a recommender shows'; the paper never mentions compaction, summaries or sub-agents. Card's inference, not the paper's: a compaction summary and an orchestrator brief are also a chosen subset of items from a pool (facts, constraints, turns) with one episode outcome, so the same counts test applies when the unit is a discrete retained item; and the conventions that void identifiability are the lane's defaults, a fixed token or item budget (the $\mathbf{h}_\emptyset$ obstacle) and one conversation compacted once (the private-store obstacle, Proposition 2: at most one item value per episode). Two things break the mapping: summaries rewrite rather than select, so the design is not 0/1 and the item unit is the summarizer's choice; and a handoff is seldom replayed across episodes, so $T_b=1$ almost always. The consistent conclusion for the lane is that per-item attribution of a compaction or handoff failure from logged outcomes needs designed variation in what is kept (paired replay with varied inclusion, which is how CL-W44-06 already proceeds), and that any 'memory value' or 'summary-item importance' reported from a fixed-budget trace without such variation is a solver's choice.
occupies: The published result that memory valuation from a retrieval log is an estimability question whose design is fixed by the retrieval and co-retrieval counts; that a fixed retrieval size leaves every memory's Shapley value undetermined at every resolution and every $T$ (no consistent estimator for binary outcomes), that $d+1$ distinct non-nested sizes on a shared store are needed, that a private store asked once determines at most one value, and that always-co-retrieved memories alias to their sum (the 'memory-reward trap' of RoMeRL named as a kernel vector); the audit that all 55 configurations of 14 standard memory benchmarks determine zero values; LEDGER (kernel test, ridge estimate with per-functional interval, merge of identical histories, size-varying least-retrieved-fill retrieval) with 0.001 to 0.797 determined on pooled HotpotQA at $-2.6$ points and $+2.7$ on LoCoMo; and the proposal that memory benchmarks report the fraction of values their logs determine alongside accuracy. It does not claim, and leaves open: a label-free query-time gate for when spreading retrieval is free (its own pre-registered gate failed), an exact $A$-optimal retrieval rule, any result at $d\ge2$ on real logs, any real-data retention or training result built on the determined values (the synthetic retention test ranks LEDGER below reward averaging), and anything about compaction summaries or sub-agent briefs.

neighbors.title: RoMeRL: Balancing Feedback Coverage and the Memory-Reward Trap in Self-Evolving Agent Memory via Reduced-Order Utility States
neighbors.trick: Compress trajectory-indexed memory utilities into a fixed-dimensional per-task state so sparse outcome feedback is not spread over an ever-growing table, and name the 'memory-reward trap' where irrelevant memories earn credit by being retrieved alongside useful ones; the paper says that trap is the kernel vector of tied memories and that no log-reading procedure can separate them.

neighbors.title: Memory-R2: Fair Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Memory-Augmented LLM Agents
neighbors.trick: Train memory operations with outcome rewards and an explicit per-operation credit rule, because rollouts that write different memories no longer share an environment and GRPO-style comparisons become unfair; the paper says that with a fixed number of retrieved memories per rollout the per-memory credit is undetermined by the rewards whatever the rule.

neighbors.title: MemLens: A Value-Aware Memory Management System with Interactive Analytics for LLM-based Agents
neighbors.trick: Define a Memory Shapley value, compute it by evaluating the system on coalitions of memories of the method's choosing, and drive retention and a dashboard from it; the paper keeps the same notion of value but asks which of these values the coalitions that actually occurred in deployment determine, with no replay.

neighbors.title: FadeMem: Biologically-Inspired Forgetting for Efficient Agent Memory
neighbors.trick: Decay each memory at an exponential rate modulated by semantic relevance, access frequency and recency across a two-layer store; the paper points out that access frequency is the diagonal of the retrieval Gram matrix, which records how often a memory is needed and decides whether its contribution can be learned but does not measure it.

neighbors.title: Off-policy evaluation for slate recommendation
neighbors.trick: Estimate a slate policy's value from logged set-valued actions by assuming the reward is a sum of per-slot effects and solving the same count-based linear system; its estimand is a policy value, for which the kernel can be projected out, while here the estimand is each item's value and the kernel is the finding.

theme_fit.why: self-written agent memory valued for what each entry contributes, in the measurement register the lane demands: an identifiability test on the traces every memory system already logs, the finding that the field's own protocols (fixed k, private stores) cannot measure memory value at all, and a small recipe consequence (shared store, varied size, break nesting) with its accuracy cost measured; the extension to compaction and handoffs is the card's inference, not the paper's

a ground-truth precondition for credit signals: RL memory agents (Memory-R1/R2, RoMeRL) fit per-memory credit from rollouts, and the paper shows that with fixed-size retrieval the rewards leave that credit undetermined and co-retrieved memories alias; an enabling piece for a definitive comparison of memory-credit methods under designed vs logged rollouts, not a new recipe

benchmark validity: an audit instrument that reads only retrieval traces, finds zero determined values in 55 configurations of 14 benchmarks, and proposes a new reported column (fraction of values the log determines) alongside accuracy; the kind of column the lane's measurers ship
no serving, cache or cost-structure content; the only cost is answer accuracy

limitations_as_complaints: My retrieval rule is a heuristic I cannot justify or make free: 'LEDGER's rule is a count-based heuristic motivated by $A$-optimal design; it optimises no criterion.' and 'Its effect on accuracy depends on the corpus, from $-2.6$ to $+2.7$ points, and the only rule that removes the cost is an oracle that needs gold labels.' (H.4); my pre-registered label-free gate failed ($+1.25$ $[0.0,+2.4]$ against ungated LEDGER, F.3) and 'Finding at query time the questions where spreading retrieval costs nothing is the open problem that remains.' (sec. 6).

Everything I report on real logs is an additive, associational number: 'The results assume that the query-averaged value has no dividends above order $d$ (Assumption 2), and the real-data experiments use $d=1$. Omitted dividends bias the estimates wherever they correlate with the design' and 'The reported values are associational unless the log is exogenous (Appendix H.1).' (H.4); at $d=2$ the design has about $4.4\times10^{6}$ columns against $T=7{,}200$, so interactions between memories are out of reach on real stores (H.1).

I cannot check my intervals where they matter and my remedy did not transfer: 'Coverage of the intervals is measured on synthetic logs drawn from the model, where the true values are known; on real logs it cannot be measured.' and 'The result that coverage holds on every reported value at $d=2$ comes from a post hoc analysis (Appendix G).' (H.4); the pre-registered test 'The remedy recovers identifiability on three audited benchmarks' 'failed: 0.46, 0.13, 0.08; falsified on MemoryAgentBench' and 'Reach is the binding ceiling' 'failed on two of three benchmarks' (Table 13).
limitation_quotes: LEDGER's rule is a count-based heuristic motivated by $A$-optimal design; it optimises no criterion. (H.4 Limitations, Retrieval)
The rule treats the $M=20$ memories most similar to the query as candidates of comparable relevance, and we did not test this assumption directly. (H.4)
Its effect on accuracy depends on the corpus, from $-2.6$ to $+2.7$ points, and the only rule that removes the cost is an oracle that needs gold labels. (H.4)
The reported values are associational unless the log is exogenous (Appendix H.1). (H.4 Limitations, Model)
Omitted dividends bias the estimates wherever they correlate with the design, and Proposition A.1 bounds only their direct effect on each value. (H.4)
Coverage of the intervals is measured on synthetic logs drawn from the model, where the true values are known; on real logs it cannot be measured. (H.4 Limitations, Estimation)
The result that coverage holds on every reported value at $d=2$ comes from a post hoc analysis (Appendix G). (H.4)
The audit runs each benchmark at one pass. (H.4 Limitations, Experiments)
The pooled stores for HotpotQA and LongMemEval are our construction; the benchmarks define private stores. (H.4)
Rules that choose sets from past outcomes, such as bandit algorithms, violate the condition of Proposition 3. (H.2)
A deployed agent has no gold labels, and the first substitute we pre-registered failed. (H.2)
Finding at query time the questions where spreading retrieval costs nothing is the open problem that remains. (sec. 6)
the pre-registered real-data retention test was not completed. (F.7)

The same test therefore applies to the tools an agent calls in an episode, the passages a retrieval-augmented generator reads, and the slates a recommender shows (Swaminathan et al., 2017), and each of these settings has its own versions of the fixed size, the private pool and the tied items. (H.2 Scope)
